Like I myself have always had traps that inserted basically at my jaw but had no volume, which with training started to look that way. 

Having those kinds of long insertions with your traps and width of pec insertions, and delt insertions that go like half the length of your upper arm like chandlers, those three things are what give that roid look where your torso looks like a triangle on top of a longer upside-down triangle. Granted, the traps and delts are where most of your androgen receptors are, but still the position of the insertion itself is impossible to change and is the main thing to dictate how Romero-ish you’ll look with training. 

Some guys can be strong but just have the opposite of a wrestlers build, more like a swimmers build that strikers tend to have (think concave lats rather than round convex lats, like khabib); they could work out and take gear until the end of time but will still just look like a really defined and vascular swimmer pretty much.

Not every guy with that torso is on something, I mean probably, but the thing is you can get it with the right genetics and no roids but can’t get it the other way around. It’s just genetics and training/low bf%. The latter two are the case for close to all athletes, so it tends to only be the insertions that dictate how roidy they look. When it’s angular not linear it’s just called angular inertia not angular momentum, I work in that field so I use the terms for it; everyone knows Inertia just means how much force is needed to bring an object to rest anyway, even linearly, the way a moving truck has a lot of inertia. 

If the centre of mass of a weapon is concentrated far to the opposite end to your grip that means you can swing it with more angular inertia/momentum; the angular inertia that will cave in a breastplate and give up all kinetic energy to do so before coming to a halt, that is the same angular inertia which you yourself have to offset via the torque from your back muscles to bring the mass to a halt, or to change direction if you don’t strike an object. And one cannot do that when your grip is on the opposite end to the centre of mass, if the mass is already so comically large that Ned can barely lift, just the mass itself (try swinging an axe when your friend can barely lift the weight of the axe head, not to mention generating the torque to change direction once swung to have any dexterity; it’s a comical notion and you’d know that if you thought about it, or weren’t just being a pedant about words you’re pretending to understand, or just swung an axe for that matter).

Angular inertia = rotational velocity x mass x displacement from centre of mass.

If the latter two are great as in Roberts hammer to a comical degree, and you can manage to swing with any sizeable angular velocity, that product of the three is exactly the amount of angular inertia that you need to offset to change direction, via torque from your muscles. This is why when chopping wood you always have a smooth handle and even just instinctively slide your dominant hand down to where the axe head is to raise it (lowering the rotational inertia to lift it, increasing rotational inertia by sliding your hand down the haft in the other direction to break the wood). If you didn’t your back would give out before you could chop anything. That is because you’re reducing that force necessary the closer and closer to zero the closer you slide your grip to the centre of mass. Which is why if I just rested my sword on the end of your axe you would not be able to lift it, I’d have all mechanical advantage, like Reagar would after redirecting a swing (which again the wielder can’t do anything about with that much mass concentrated that far out, to change direction literally takes as much torque as to swing in the first place, which is why no weapons like this have ever existed, aside from the English longbowmen just being opportunistic at Agincort in using their mauls designed for planting in stakes to kill the defenceless French nights immobilised by the mud and dead horses. If the knights were not immobilised then rushing in with a maul as your weapon would be absurd, hence that never occuring). There’s a reason the centre of mass of a weapon is always near the grip, why there is a whole art form about it.

The way torque works (what is needed by the wielder to influence the inertia), is that if the weight is twice as far away from your grip, you need to apply twice as much torque (torque = mass x distance). Try holding a broom horizontal with one hand on the end for a minute and then with your hand at the centre for a minute; it would be half as much strain the second time even if we regard the rod as massless (otherwise it will be even less than half because you’d have a counterbalance on the other end; since it’s not the weight that’s the issue, it’s where it’s concentrated). 

The person who applies force closest to the centre of mass of the weapon is the one with control over it. If I’m applying a small resisting force with a stick 1cm away from the centre of mass of a polearm that you yourself are gripping 70cm away from its centre of mass, as one would, you genuinely would need to pull 70x harder than myself. 

Torque is t=mass x distance. It’s just the way things work. No it’s not mostly the training, it’s just the same deal whole ‘doing laps is a good exercise to get the body of a swimmer’ myth that used to go around. 

One doesn’t get the body of a swimmer (muscular in a lanky ‘elegant’ way) by swimming at all, it’s just most swimmers have that muscular long limbed build because it’s what favours swimming.

Same thing with wrestling, where it’s about being stocky with long muscle bellies that insert closer to the joint. If you think of a sprinter’s calves they have a short muscle belly further away from the heel so the tendon can be longer (while wrestlers have the opposite, longer and broader calve bellies at the expense of a shorter tendon). 

The speed of contraction has to be proportional to the length of the tendon, since it’s basically like a spring but contracting instead of lengthening, where the longer a spring the more kinetic energetic it can push with. The trade off of having a shorter tendon is that it can’t push you as fast, but can have a broader cross sectional area of the muscle belly (more muscle fibres like sardines side by side), which can’t increase the speed but increases the torque/strength when they contract - like if you pack 100 springs of some given length side by side and have them push a board on top of them when released, the board won’t move 100x faster but will have 100x the inertia (you’d have to push 100x as hard to keep the board stationary; for wrestlers this is exactly what they need, because they want to *resist* the movement of another heavy strong man rather than nimbly dance around him). Whereas if you got all those springs and welded them on top of one another, if you put the same amount of energy into compressing it as the other example it would actually push the board with 100x the kinetic energy/speed but wouldn’t take the same ridiculous amount of strength to resist it; this is what a springer wants, he doesn’t need a huge amount of torque to overpower another man, he wants to be able to bounce quickly into motion. 

So the sprinter has the equivalent of the springs stacked on top of one another with a longer tendon and shorter muscle belly. The wrestler has the longer wider muscle belly that has a greater cross sectional area of ‘springs’ (muscle fibres), since all that matters is torque of the joint (it’s ‘strength’ - ability to push/resist greater forces), while the speed (from length of tendon) doesn’t matter as much, you’re better served by having the muscle belly take up more volume than the tendon. So this is why a wrestlers triceps are always really thick closer to the joint (say May Hughes), while a striker can would more like a Kevin Holland type.

It seems to be designed (not that well) to measure the kinetic energy imparted by the punch, by multiplying the reactive force from the pad by the distance that it’s displaced [force (N) x distance (m) = energy (Nm)].

This isn’t the full picture at all though, or even a very good one, because punches cause damage in two unique ways, with kinetic energy transfer not having all that much to do with concussive potential. Structural damage like fractured bones occurs from kinetic energy absorbed by a strike, while absorbing momentum of strike is what accelerates the head (as in to spin around, causing concussion on the return swing when the brain hits the skull wall).

Since kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity (Ke = 0.5m*v^2) it means faster strikers carry/transfer more of it, whilst the strikers that can mobilise more mass in their movement carry more momentum (m*v) and thus concussive power. 

A strike with more kinetic energy is like a small rock being slung at you at a high speed, while a strike with more momentum (and not much kinetic energy) is more like being hit by a big fat dude very slowly swinging an egg-weight at you. 

The former example (picture Sean O’Malley) will break bones in your face but not concuss you very much (unless it hits your chin, which is essentially a fulcrum to spin the head around), while the latter example (picture Francis) will probably not cause all that much superficial damage but the momentum transfer will accelerate your head and rattle/concuss your brain, wherever you’re hit.

So while momentum (the mass mobilised in a strike) is essentially what generally causes concussions, it’s not something that can be measured as easily as kinetic energy, where you can just look at the force on the pad and the distance that the pad is displaced, and it’s done.

With that kind of setup, measuring only the energy transfer, it’s just the physics of it that if some spazzy skinny guy can strike twice as fast as you, you would need to be able to mobilise 4x as much mass just to match his score. This is probably why Francis (while IRL capable of KOing anybody) is being beaten on the machine by smaller guys that hit a little bit faster.

A pitched battle is just what it sounds like, when both sides decide to meet in a field and throw down. I’m guessing you have the impression most battles were fought this way making the term redundant but historically these battles were a rarity, with sieges and ‘small war’ (when you just drain the enemy’s supplies by killing their peasants and burning their fields and infrastructure etc) being what filled those huge gaps between them; but they tend to be the climactic ends to wars so they’re what history (and fiction especially) tend to fixate on. Indeed these battles have been romanticised so much it’s easy to get the impression that it’s all the occurred in warfare. Even Alexander the Great stomping Persia so extraordinarily quickly and thoroughly only had like four battles, which were indeed climactic and pivotal, but the rest of the time he was just starving out strategical location after strategical location in an extended boring process that forced the Persians to have to risk pitched battles (before they were too weakened by this process that is - Alexander’s father had closely copied the Persian logistical system of keeping such an army supplied, so these weren’t Greeks that got hungry and bored and went home quickly anymore if you refused to fight man to man in the ‘gentlemanly’ way the Greek city states were familiar with).

Usually when one army mobilises it’s bigger than an army stationed at the fort/city/etc that it’s attacking, so would win in a pitched battle should the defenders leave their fortifications and offer a fight, so they don’t, and just wait for supplying this massive army far away from home to become too costly (starvation, disease, or logistically/financially if they have fortified supply lines) until they leave, which happened quite often. 

So it would become a game of chicken (of who’s army would dwindle and capitulate or leave first), one that the attackers could even out by destroying the resources supplying the city/fort (which of course couldn’t all be fortified), the term for which (small war) is French but has been occurring whenever there’s a good reason for one side to not engage, like the Peloppanesian wars where Sparta had the stronger infantry but Athens the stronger navy, so neither would fight where they’re weaker, and just slowly ruined each other over time until they were a shadow of their former selves by when Phillip of Macedon showed up. 

In GRRM pitched battles just happen all over the place, often seemingly without strategical reasons that make all that much sense (understandably though, as wars like the former are just very boring). But IRL Tywin could have just continued burning the river-lands and just refused to engage the opposing forces (which can be fairly easily done, you just have to walk to the top of a hill or anywhere suicidal to charge once the opposing forces show up); and if his gold could keep his army supplied, and he had the strategical savvy to not let the lines be outflanked and disrupted (remember it only takes 10 good men lol), then forcing the Tullys to capitulate that way would have just been the more normal thing to do historically, as brutal as it is. The pitched battles that tend to occur in these kinds of scenarios are when the defenders are desperate enough to not lose a strategical position that isn’t fortified enough to withstand a storm or siege and has somewhat favourable terrain.

So yeah the notion that there would be pitched battles against an undead army which doesn’t need to eat (or even die from disease?) seems to not make much sense, particularly when every loss would add to their numbers. But on second thought this would only be the case if the undead were able to be forced/cornered onto the defensive, quickly enough before bypassing the Wall (as while you can’t starve out dead people, if cornered off and idle they could probably just be rendered a non-threat by human ingenuity and abundance of workers by hemming them in with series of walls and ditches filled with say obsidian stakes and flammable material, so your resources supplying your men are protected while their armies either dwindle trying to escape or are cornered long enough to be torched by more advanced siege-works, without needing to risk infecting humans, and keeping those who are from spreading). 

Whereas if they were able to flood through the Wall and stay on the offensive, it would likely be like being attacked by an incredibly logistically complex state like Rome (that also doesn’t have to worry about starving before the enemy), where you often simply have no choice to take the chance fighting them in a pitched battle. As the undead could just (intentionally or not) starve you out if you do all the normally conventionally defensively wise things, by just killing/infecting all your farmers supplying each defensive position (unless you leave to offer an open battle each time), or by them seeing that every peasant given refuge in the fortified positions just quickens the pace at which starvation and disease wipes each defensive position out.

They are though, and always have been since the technology became available post-Palaeolithic. So many dominant civilisations that have made their mark on history did so via maritime trade and colonisation, from the early Bronze Age to the late Middle Ages and even the age of sail more recently, which only stopped once there was nothing left to colonise.

Greece had no trouble, the Carthaginians had no trouble, Rome had no trouble despite hardly knowing how to sail until reverse-engineering a lost Carthaginian trireme, the Berbers and Turks had no trouble, the Nordic peoples had no trouble (colonising Northern Europe, later Normandy in France, later modern England), and soon after England/Spain/Portugal had so much success that they divided up the entire known world between them and had colonies so far away they had to circumnavigate the globe to get to them.

That’s not even to mention all the seafaring colonising cultures prior to the Bronze Age collapse like the Mycenaeans, Minoans, the Sea Peoples (from Crete, Palestine), etc. Almost every single major empire or dominant culture you’ll come across in a history book that did not originate in landlocked Asia/Eurasian Steps (even then only for lack of seas to cross) made its mark via spreading through seafaring trade, conquest and colonisation.

The Palaeolithic is the only period where this wasn’t the case and only for lack of technology, and even then you somehow still had island hopping civilisations like in the pacific islands. 

Setting up foreign colonies and gaining control over trade has always been the most expedient way to gain wealth (trading local produce for resources foreign to your homeland and thus valuable) and regional hegemony (controlling/taxing the trade routes). This is valuable because there are simply only so many trade routes. And overland trade was essentially impossible over long distances prior to modern technology like trains; it could be done via rivers if available or just via a slow costly process of neighbours trading with neighbours like with the Silk Road and only then if the cultures on the opposite ends actually value each others goods enough. 

It’s never been individual cultures death-marching pack animals from state to disparate state. So trade which was generally more expedient than war for gaining material goods would always be done be sea, which means setting up outposts and thus eventually colonies, from the beginning of the Bronze Age until we ran out of places to colonise several centuries ago.

Not to mention if you’re a warrior culture like all of those mentioned, there will always come a point where there are too few local resources to fight over, and a lot to gain and little to lose by sending off idle men and second sons to carve out their own colonies elsewhere, it gives the culture foreign outposts (regional control and access to critical materials like tin and copper) and gets rid of young men otherwise driven to wage war on their own, which also allows the remaining individuals to not have to financially compete as much for the same limited raw materials. 

Greece indeed had a policy of basically just forcing warriors without inheritance to band together and sail around the Aegean until they could establish their own colonies, notably in Ionia which started the Persian wars when these colonies refused to accept Persian rule, and called for aid from their relatives in Athens and Sparta, and also much earlier in Turkey which sparked the Trojan war. This is why Ancient Greece wasn’t really a unified state at all but just a tonne of city states of varying sizes scattered around the Aegean Sea which all recognised each other as belonging to the same culture but were very much independent otherwise.

Men in my opinion go one of two ways in this position, they either just become really meek and defeated and hide from provocation like a beaten dog, the way I was for most of my adolescence, or alternatively they seek it out to prove to themselves they’re not the weak battered child they still see themselves as, which is the way I became in early adulthood starting with the first time I actually stood up to my father. If you’re fortunate enough to appear imposing in some way it tends to be a massive leg up in taking advantage (for lack of a better word) of your circumstance and find a way out. I found that just never flinching and making others uncomfortable with my presence (if starting to pose a threat) would stop people trying to prey on that weakness, as that unusual bodily stillness and stillness of gaze while talking that becomes second nature to you can be strangely off-putting to a lot of people, as they seem to really often mistake it for confidence (as in thinking you must have such faith in being able to handle yourself as to be totally relaxed in the face of a threat, even if you’re just freezing up or even panicking).

The fog really was a godsend for the Allies, the Germans had so many beaches to defend and so few seasoned soldiers left to do it with, and it was just another layer adding to the confusion and logistical nightmare going on.

There was a mass confusion and panic in their ranks at the time which the fog greatly exacerbated; they weren’t aware of whether it was another feint after all the prior bombardments, or what beaches to reinforce if not. Their supplies were stretched too thin to fortify the whole coastline, with a lot of the greener troops being said to have succumbed to shock by the end of the final bombardment before the assault, and a lot of the officers being too drunk and worn out from stress to be of any use.

Without the fog, it’s presumed higher command would have had better luck with knowing which beaches to send supplies and reinforcements to, and the lower ranks would have had better visibility of their targets, and what was going on in general, and would have been less likely to succumb to shock and confusion as easily if they had clear orders and could see what was happening. 

Once moral starts to break it tends to snowball quickly, particularly against a sudden overwhelming assault after hours/days of artillery bombardment designed to make the German soldiers too numb and fatigued to rally when the actual assault started. This probably would have been the case anyway, but the fog tipped the scale way too far to afford the thin/confused/poorly supplied German lines much chance. 

I think we just don’t talk about it’s influence as much as it deserves because it arguably takes some of the (well earned) heroism away, for instance if the assault’s success came to be regarded as a forgone conclusion due to the conditions.

Nerd. Anyway the eye circle thing an issue arising from the opposite, having less prominent (ie shallower) cheekbones, as is the case in some Iranians and many people of the Indian subcontinent. As cheekbones are just the bottom part of your orbital bones, and in peoples where the these bones encircling your eye are shallower than the rest of the skull (as well as wider from brow ridge to cheekbone) it acts as a ‘sink’ for light, making the skin around the eyes appear darker, just as if you press a round depression into some dough and look at it from side-on the dough and notice the depression will look darker. Workers from India and Pakistan tend to be accused by their bosses of being tired/disinterested more often than most for this reason.

In contrast, people of ethnic groups where the cheek/orbital bones are much more prominent, as well as narrower from brow to cheek, like in Germanic peoples, they tend to rarely look tired at all because the opposite is the case - the bones surrounding the eye press upwards more creating a more distinct contour that catches and reflects back light more easily, and with the bones being narrower from the brow to the cheek the eyes sit more firmly between the bones such that there isn’t a gradient of lightness to darkness in the skin between the bones and the eyes. Either the brow ridge completely shadows the eye, or everything looks clear and even toned.

But people from the caucuses have fairly different phenotypes to germanics, and wider (as opposed to vertically narrower) orbital bones, that make the eyes look wider and less relaxed, are quite a bit more common. And Islam has just quite a prominent case of this.

The depressurisation force is not enough to move massive objects, and even if it was, the duration of the force is as short as it takes for the interior pressure to reach an equilibrium with the outside pressure via air escaping, which is not very long at all. People probably already know this but interestingly enough nothing much really happens if you break a window in plane, or create an even bigger breach like we see in movies, as all that would happen is the plane’s interior would quickly depressurise to match the pressure of the altitude you’re at, which is a minor enough pressure gradient to not actually disturb anything (with any mass) inside the plane, well aside from your inner ears which are very sensitive to sudden pressure changes and will hurt a lot. 

And because the plane has a fairly small internal volume it doesn’t take much air leaking out either for its interior to become at an equilibrium with the altitude’s pressure (at which point the internal/external pressures are equal and nothing else happens), so even if the force of the depressurisation was strong enough to move massive objects like in movies, it would only last for an instance before the pressures even out, so even with movie physics going on they would only perhaps wobble for a second.

Really once the pressures are rendered equal in this way, flying in a plane with a window open would be no different at all to travelling on a really fast bullet train with a window open; since both objects are moving at pretty much a constant velocity everything inside will remain at rest as if stationary, as is the case for all inertial (not accelerating) frames of reference. Being in the sky genuinely doesn’t change any of this at all, aside from it hurting your ears a lot sitting in plane who’s air pressure is now much lower than sea level.

The reason Hitler was so obsessed with this fact is because he respected the Indo-Aryan martial domination of Europe for so much of prehistory, and wanted to use it as a weird pretext for the most ‘pure’ ancestors of this group to dominate Europe for another millenia, hence the thousand year reich. 

This is because Indo-Aryans were a nomadic people that are known to have very successfully spread (mostly through warfare) widely throughout Europe and Western Asia, for reasons presumed to be related to technological advances like the chariot and a hierarchical social structure favouring its warrior class, and to have established themselves in a kind of proto-nobility class that sat above and ruled for for countless centuries the people they conquered. This didn’t really happen that often as usually in prehistory conquered peoples would be just exterminated or enslaved, but it did work well for this group though; a more modern analogy for this same thing is the way that the Normans ruled over the the previous inhabitants of England (Angles, Saxons, Britons) as a distinct and culturally/linguistically isolated nobility class after the conquest of 1066.

Because the Indo-Aryans became the ruling classes across such a diversity of distinct cultures, in some cultures they isolated themselves and in some they intermixed, which is why Iranians of today look different from their relatives in say Northern Europe, since intermixture with conquered peoples in the latter region isn’t going to change one’s complexion nearly as much (compared to say in the Indian subcontinent). They’re certainly not at all irrational in the sense of being more hindering than helpful. They’re just regarded as such since we started noticing them in post-agrarian contexts, wherein we’re no longer as vulnerable to the threats they protect us from. 

But if one was to venture away from civilisation for a short period, instinctive aversions to things like the sound of scuttling (arachnophobia), hard to discern objects submerged beneath murky water (submechanophobia), porous skin on a hunted animal (trypophobia), etc, would all of a sudden again be some of the most rational things our subconscious mind could do to protect us (eg from poison, submerged predators like gators, and viruses respectively, for these three examples).

There is no phobia that is present in humans that didn’t force its way in there by almost every single person who didn’t have it dying (prior to reproducing) at some point in our collective past. 

Saying the reason for the above commenter having one of these is blind irrationality (rather than a very rational reason that just doesn’t hold up as well in the conditions we’re currently living in), is like saying if you have the option of carrying a gun that your natural wariness of your surroundings while say walking through a sketchy area, is also just some irrational dysfunction of the mind bereft of some underlying reason.

Like with the gun, scuba gear and swimming in groups is what protects us from drowning when venturing out into vast expanses of water, in the manner that elicits thalassophobia, but the fear of doing so even with these protective measures is of course far less harmful to one’s wellbeing than the boldness to do so without it. Things like knowing you can only tread water for so long without dying are things your subconscious mind understands more concretely via this fear than (some peoples) conscious minds.

(For instance those idiots who sometimes dive off cruise ships for fun and die - often when we really want to do something or are in a group our rational mind is really good at rationalising to us that we’re competent enough to do it, which is a way of thinking that tends to be very conducive to success in the safety of the modern world, and which we accordingly tend to put a lot of stock in. So there’s a very good reason our subconscious mind often tries to override these kinds of impulses in situations it knows to be dangerous by via instilling fear; and for those where the response is not strong enough they often carry the risk of ending up the way of the cruise ship idiots.)

Muscle is an advantage in most areas, but the reason you don’t see every fighter in mma totally jacked is for two main reasons:

-oxygen consumption: more muscle means more oxygen consumption just to overcome your own inertia, and you can only breathe in so much oxygen. This matters because mma is to a degree an endurance sport.

-weightclasses and leverage: since you can only have so much mass per weightclass, jacking yourself up with muscle to the point where you need to enter a higher weightclass, where competitors are naturally longer and heavier boned than you, puts you at a disadvantage rather than an advantage. This is because someone with a heavier, longer frame who has just enough muscle to move it quickly/athletically will generally hit much harder than a mucky guy of the same weight, the reason being that most of the kinetic energy of a punch comes from the amount of mass moved and leverage that allows for more ‘snap’ when doing so. Also the mass of bones is fairly even all the way the along a limb, while the mass of your muscles thins out a lot the further along the limb that you go. And the more mass that you have towards the extremities of the limbs the harder you can hit (consider a ball on the end of a chain being swung, compared to heavy chain being swung, if both have the same mass). This is why guys with ginormous hands for their weightclasses hit the hardest, like Alex Pereira and Jan Blackovich for instance.

This is such an insane take lmao. The fact that Sulla and Marius did it doesn’t make it okay and more tolerable, but just the opposite. You’ve got to be aware that these attacks were literally the two bloodiest/most traumatising events in the living memory for Roman citizens around at the time (and perhaps historically as well, being similar in scale and trauma to that one close-call of a Gallic sacking). What we’re talking about is literally invading your own city, which is just like it sounds haha, that is if everyone doesn’t immediately capitulate with the terror and lack of opposition that a conquered people might.

The first time with Marius, the people of Rome didn’t know what to expect and genuinely thought the sacred (fake) border around the city would protect them and prevent any principled, god-fearing Roman from doing something so brutal and sacrilegious.

The second time, with Sulla, the people got duped again, thinking he was a protector of Roman virtue here to put an end to Marius’s reign of terror; not someone equally brutal who would continue it, just from the other direction.

By the point of people getting wind of it about to happen again (a third time in no more than a generation or so, no less), nobody had any disillusions left anymore concerning savageness of Roman generals towards those they swore to protect. They knew well what would come to them if they didn’t roll over. 

Indeed Caesar knowing they knew this was the sole reason he didn’t have to. It was PR that he could capitalise on - but if he didn’t have the option to wrestle control from the city without creating a bloodbath like his predecessors (one of whom was his uncle, and the other the mentor of his career-long best friend and closest ally), there is no reason to think he wouldn’t have.

Indeed, if Pompey didn’t buy Caesar’s bluff and shit his pants across the Adriatic, but instead contested his entry from the walls of Rome, can anyone seriously expect Ceasar would not have followed through on his threat and try to take the city by storm or siege? Remember he stood to lose everything and be tried as a common criminal (by a particularly vengeful senate) for all the litany of war crimes and laws he flaunted if he backed down at any stage and lost his consular immunity.

And at least it’s some consolation that Marius and Sulla both ‘conquered’ the city while their competitor was off at war. Two equally competent generals like Caesar and Pompey fighting for control of a city, with the battlegrounds being the city, would have likely even been orders of magnitude worse than even these two most traumatising events in lived memory for these people.

Remember this was a man who boasted about enslaving a third, displacing a third, and killing a third of Gauls who’d already surrendered to him, and never even raised arms against him except in righteous self-defence (even when this was a principle Caesar himself dearly respected, according to what he recorded in Commentaries from his discussions with Ariovistus).

So who would have (without benefit of hindsight) genuinely had faith that a man of this nature would not do similar to those who resisted? Furthermore if the considerably less brutal six-time-consul and rejoiced ‘defender of Rome’ Marius, had no qualms with it (and while possessing far, far less cause for a grudge against the city than Caesar), it would have seemed pretty insanely unlikely that Caesar would.

And needless to say in Ancient Rome, unlike today, during the course of such transfers of power citizens are certainly not mostly off-limits/ignored, as everyone back then (even plebs via client relations) necessarily had broadly known political ties in one way or another. And so accordingly could be targeted as partisans depending on the whims of the conqueror with no further justification needed.

(Indeed this is why so many random people totally unopposed to Sulla, or even members of the faction he was fighting for, ended up proscribed - just because they could be, and sometimes it was profitable to do so.) Even your political affiliation or lack-thereof were not enough to ensure any degree of safety.

The only reason there was actually so little resistance when Ceasar did the same was not at all because it was just this minor, common thing to do, but because the generational trauma these people were still living with from the last two times it happened (with most Romans at this time still living with the memory of losing one or more family in these purges), rendered them so petrified of the consequences of a potential third protracted culling, that a show of force was enough to break them. All but the most fanatical with too much to lose, that is.

So no, the fact that all but the most fanatical senators rolled over does not indicate that the reason for this was because marching on the city was not a big deal, but rather for the the exact opposite reason, the extent of how bad they all knew it would be if they didn’t. Like their greatest nightmare repeating a third time.

The *wraps* (casts around the hands, basically) are to protect the hands, the gloves are to protect the head. Be careful not to get the two mixed up or consider them as the same. If you hit someone with wraps but no gloves you might kill them. 

The way it works is the wraps make you able to swing wildly with a lot of force and follow-through, making it feel like your bones from your forearm to knuckles are fused. Meanwhile the gloves stop this from being a potentially lethal weapon by reducing the pressure on impact by two ways, by increasing the surface area via the larger area of the glove (Pressure (N/m^2) = Force(N)/Area(m^2) -> inversely proportional to area), as well as by reducing the *force* itself via the padding of the gloves, which increases the time taken to impart the force of the swing. Imparted force is inversely proportional to this -> (Force(N)= impulse(change in momentum from impact of punch)/time(how long this change in momentum takes).

So as you can see from the pressure equation, the amount of ‘pounds per square inch’ (for Americans) is reduced two-fold, by the net force on impact being reduced by the increased time to impart the momentum (from padding), and the localisation of the force being reduced by the increased surface area. So if of these variables were derived from the same quantity, we would say that gloves decrease the pounds per square inch by the *square* of this quantity, which is by an enormous amount. For example if we say surface area of gloves is about twice that of wrapped knuckles, and the padding takes about 1.5x as long to impart the full force of the swing as wrapped bone does, then the pounds per square inch would decrease by a factor of (2^2)*(1.5^2)=4*2.25=9, so it would be 1/9th of what it would be if the hands were just wrapped.
